title: The 1920 Franchise Is Back to Haunt You. Vikram Bhatt and Anand Pandit Reunite for 1920: Cold Winter.
excerpt: India's most durable horror brand returns for another candlelit haunting — the eighth chapter in a saga that has been scaring the diaspora for eighteen years.
body:
There is a certain kind of Indian horror that doesn't need a jump scare to get under your skin — it just needs a candlelit haveli, a woman with kohl-smudged eyes turning slowly toward the camera, and a year on the title card that tells you this story is old enough to have outlived everyone in it. For nearly two decades, that year has been 1920. And on June 19, the franchise that taught a generation of Indian filmgoers to sleep with the lights on confirmed it is coming back for another haunting.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=HPSXqrd-ykA

Filmmaker Vikram Bhatt — the man who started it all — and producer Anand Pandit have officially reunited for 1920: Cold Winter, the newest chapter in one of Indian cinema's most durable horror brands. The title alone is doing a lot of work: after a saga that has wandered through possessed havelis, colonial London and tortured romances, "Cold Winter" promises a chillier, bleaker register — the kind of setting where the dread comes from the silence and the frost as much as from whatever is lurking in the corridor.

The timing is no accident. The announcement lands hot on the heels of Haunted 3D: Echoes of the Past, which hit cinemas on June 12, 2026, and gave Bhatt and Pandit the momentum to revive their crown-jewel series. Bhatt will write and direct Cold Winter himself — fitting, given he helmed the 2008 original — while Pandit produces, with Roopa Pandit and Rahul V Dubey as co-producers.

The 1920 franchise has built its loyal fanbase on one reliable promise: horror laced with romance, mystery and the supernatural — gothic melodrama with a beating heart.

To understand why this matters, you have to understand how unusual it is for an Indian horror property to last this long. 1920 began in 2008 with Adah Sharma and Rajniesh Duggall, a story about a man who abandons his family and his faith only to find his wife possessed by a demonic force. It was a genuine hit — a rarity for the genre at the time — and it established a template the series has returned to again and again: love, betrayal, and something monstrous wearing a familiar face.

What followed was a small empire. 1920: Evil Returns arrived in 2012 with Aftab Shivdasani, Sharad Kelkar and Tia Bajpai. 1920 London: Fear Strikes Again (2016) moved the chills abroad with Sharman Joshi and Meera Chopra. 1921 (2018) conjured a fresh supernatural tale set in England, led by Karan Kundrra and Zareen Khan. And in 2023, 1920: Horrors of the Heart — directed by Krishna Bhatt, written by Mahesh Bhatt, and starring Avika Gor and Randheer Rai — handed the franchise to a new generation. Cold Winter now extends a bloodline of scares that has survived shifting tastes, the streaming revolution, and the rise and fall of a dozen flashier horror trends.

Plot details are being kept firmly under wraps, which is exactly how the Bhatt camp likes it — let the title and the period atmosphere do the teasing. But the formula is unlikely to change: a haunted setting steeped in period detail, a love story that curdles, and a possession that forces someone to fight for the soul of the person they love most. It is gothic comfort food, and the 1920 faithful have never wanted anything else.

For the diaspora, the Bhatt horror universe occupies a specific, nostalgic corner of the heart. These were the films that played on satellite TV and pirated DVDs in living rooms from Edison to Hounslow, the ones cousins dared each other to finish at sleepovers, the soundtracks — all aching, minor-key melodies — that somehow stayed in the bloodstream. A new 1920 isn't just another horror release; for a certain NRI generation, it's a portal back to a very particular flavour of growing up with Hindi cinema.

There is no release date or full cast yet, and given the franchise's habit of period settings and atmospheric slow-builds, Cold Winter will likely take its time. But the brand carries weight: a 1920 film travels, and overseas distributors know it. Expect it to surface on the diaspora theatrical circuit when it lands, with streaming to follow on one of the Indian-content platforms — the same path that has kept the series alive for new audiences for eighteen years and counting.

For now, all we have is a title, a reunited creative duo, and the cold certainty that somewhere in a fog-bound haveli, the candles are being lit again. The lights, for the rest of us, can stay on a while longer.
